strengths: Compelling intermediate representation: Leveraging 360-degree panoramic equirectangular renderings effectively resolves the challenge of viewing direction selection in 2D-to-3D visual grounding while preserving holistic spatial relationships among objects across the entire room.

Comprehensive technical framework: The combination of structure-aware viewpoint placement, multi-modal feature adaptation (injecting geometry and lifted 3D DINOv2 semantics via zero-convolutions), EMD digit loss for coordinate regression, and cross-view geometric verification forms a coherent, well-engineered pipeline.

Strong experimental results: The method achieves state-of-the-art results on challenging human-annotated benchmarks (e.g., Nr3D with +4.7% improvement over prior SOTA, and top performance on ScanRefer).

Insightful generalization experiments: The paper demonstrates strong robustness on cross-dataset transfers (ARKitScenes and 3RScan) and against linguistic perturbations (e.g., outperforming baselines by +15.9% on affordance queries without class names), highlighting the power of transferring rich 2D VLM reasoning to 3D.

Thorough ablations: The comparisons between panoramic and pinhole cameras (especially broken down by the number of objects mentioned in the query), the study of camera placement scoring factors, and the comparison between mesh and 3DGS representations are informative and clearly validate the design choices.
weaknesses: Substantial computational and inference overhead: The pipeline relies on a heavy 17B VLM backbone (CogVLM) and requires test-time augmentation (averaging 2.4 camera positions × 4 in-place yaw rotations ≈ 9.6 forward passes per query), leading to an online inference time of ~3.3 seconds on an NVIDIA A100 GPU.

Reliance on axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) fitting: In Step 3 of the 3D aggregation stage, an axis-aligned bounding box is fitted to the unprojected point cluster. In cluttered indoor scenes where objects are oriented at arbitrary yaw angles, an AABB can be loose and prone to overlapping with neighboring objects.

Dependence on high-quality 3D reconstruction and feature pre-computation: The framework requires a pre-existing complete 3D surface (mesh or 3DGS), rendered depth maps, and an aggregated 3D semantic field pre-computed from multi-view DINOv2 features, which restricts applicability in online or strictly RGB-D stream settings.

strengths: Compelling intermediate representation: Employing 360-degree panoramic equirectangular renderings effectively bridges 2D VLMs with 3D scene understanding, avoiding the need for explicit viewing direction selection while retaining long-range spatial and relational context between objects within a single image.

Well-motivated multimodal adapter and training objective: The integration of 3D geometry (range maps) and lifted semantic feature fields via zero-initialized adapters, combined with distance-aware EMD loss and self-supervised geometric QA pre-tuning, allows the 2D VLM to effectively adapt to 3D-aware perception without catastrophic forgetting.

Strong benchmark performance: Achieves state-of-the-art results on human-annotated benchmarks including Nr3D (74.6% vs. 69.9% prior best) and ScanRefer (61.0%), demonstrating notable strength in complex multi-object scenes.

Comprehensive generalization and ablation studies: The paper provides thorough cross-dataset evaluations (ARKitScenes, 3RScan), linguistic perturbations (noun masking, affordance rewrites via LLaMA 3.3), and detailed ablations comparing panoramic views against varying pinhole camera configurations and 3D representations (Mesh vs. 3DGS).
weaknesses: Computational overhead and inference latency: The framework requires multi-view panoramic rendering, feature lifting, running a 17B VLM across multiple camera locations and test-time yaw rotations (averaging ~9.6 VLM forward passes per query), and 2D-to-3D mask unprojection with SAM, resulting in a total online runtime of ~3.30s per query on an A100 GPU (excluding offline camera placement and rendering).

Dependency on dense renderable 3D representations: The method strictly requires pre-reconstructed triangle meshes or trained 3DGS models with trajectory metadata to place cameras and render depth/RGB/feature maps, which limits applicability in sparse or uncalibrated point cloud settings where traditional 3DVG models can operate directly.

Backbone scale disparity in benchmark comparison: The main model is built on CogVLM-17B, which is substantially larger in parameter count and capacity than many traditional supervised baselines that rely on lightweight BERT/RoBERTa and PointNet++/Sparse Conv backbones. While modern MLLM-based baselines are included, a clearer discussion on parameter and compute trade-offs would provide better context.

strengths: Compelling intermediate representation: Leveraging 360-degree equirectangular panoramic views as a bridge between 3D scenes and 2D VLMs neatly preserves global spatial relationships and scene-wide context without requiring complex 3D-specific tokenization architectures.

Comprehensive and well-designed pipeline: The structure-aware camera placement (accounting for ray coverage, obstacle avoidance, and trajectory fidelity), zero-initialized multi-modal adapter (injecting geometry and lifted semantics into specific ViT depths), and visibility-aware lifting/aggregation form a cohesive framework.

Strong experimental performance: Achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results across standard 3DVG benchmarks (ScanRefer, Nr3D, Sr3D), showing particularly strong improvements on human-annotated queries (Nr3D: +4.7% over previous art).

Thorough generalization and robustness analysis: Demonstrates noticeable resilience against distribution shift when transferred to unseen datasets (ARKitScenes, 3RScan) and against linguistic perturbations (rephrasing, affordances, masked class names), outperforming strong baselines like PQ3D when explicit class cues are removed.

Extensive ablation studies: The paper and supplementary material provide detailed experiments validating design choices, including camera selection criteria, panorama vs. pinhole FoV comparisons, modality contributions, EMD loss, test-time yaw augmentations, and mesh vs. 3DGS representations.
weaknesses: High computational and inference footprint: Relying on CogVLM-17B combined with SAM unprojection across multiple panoramic viewpoints and yaw augmentations results in an online runtime of ~3.30s per query on an A100 GPU, which is substantially heavier than point-based one-stage detectors and may hinder real-time robotics applications.

Model scale disparity in benchmark comparisons: While the paper compares against other MLLM-based methods (e.g., Chat-Scene, UniVLG, LLaVA-3D), it also heavily compares against lightweight specialized 3D grounding backbones (e.g., BUTD-DETR, MCLN) without explicitly controlling or standardizing for parameter size differences.

Dependence on renderable representations and trajectory metadata: The method requires a watertight mesh or pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scene, as well as the original capture trajectory to compute distance-to-trajectory (Dtraj). Its applicability is therefore restricted when raw, unposed point clouds or unstructured 3D scans are provided.

strengths: Well-motivated use of panoramic representations: Using 360-degree panoramic renderings as an intermediate interface between 3D scenes and 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) effectively resolves the narrow field-of-view problem inherent to perspective pinhole renderings, enabling VLMs to capture holistic scene-wide relations and spatial context within very few views.

Comprehensive and modular framework design: The proposed three-stage system—structure-aware camera placement, multi-modal feature adapter (injecting depth and multi-view semantic features with zero-convolution), and visibility-aware 3D aggregation with anchor view selection—is cohesive, sound, and technically well-developed.

Impressive grounding accuracy: PanoGrounder achieves state-of-the-art results on both human-annotated Nr3D (74.6% overall vs. 69.9% for ViewSRD) and ScanRefer (61.0% overall single-dataset), with notable improvements in challenging multi-distractor and relational subsets.

Extensive robustness and generalization evaluations: The paper goes beyond standard in-domain benchmarks by evaluating cross-dataset transfer (on ARKitScenes and 3RScan), zero-shot performance against much larger models (GPT-4V and Qwen2-VL-72B), and linguistic perturbations (paraphrases, affordance-based queries, and noun masking via LLaMA 3.3).

Thorough ablation studies and practical deployment analysis: The ablation experiments rigorously isolate the benefits of each module (EMD loss, geometric/semantic adapters, camera placement heuristics, panorama vs. pinhole). Additionally, the supplementary material includes valuable real-world testing on iPhone-captured video reconstructed with 3DGS, along with latency and scalability measurements across multiple model sizes.
weaknesses: Equirectangular distortion effects: Equirectangular projections naturally suffer from non-uniform geometric distortion, particularly at high and low latitude bands. While the authors evaluate performance across elevation angles and mention that camera placement mitigates extreme distortions, the paper lacks exploration or discussion of distortion-aware projection alternatives (e.g., cubemaps, tangent patches, or distortion-corrected attention mechanisms) for 2D VLMs trained primarily on rectilinear images.

Multi-step inference pipeline complexity: The full pipeline relies on multiple external components (SAM for 2D masking, multi-view ViT feature aggregation, depth unprojection, and test-time augmentation across 4 rotations per camera), resulting in approximately 9.6 VLM forward passes per query and around 3.3s online inference per query for the 17B model.

Dependency on high-fidelity 3D reconstruction: While the supplementary material demonstrates that 3DGS from raw RGB video works, quantitative accuracy drops when moving from ground-truth meshes to fully automated reconstructions (3DGS* drops from 61.6% to 55.1% Acc@0.25), indicating sensitivity to reconstruction artifacts, floaters, and incomplete coverage.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated framework: Leveraging 360-degree panoramic renderings as an explicit 2D–3D intermediate interface effectively bridges 2D vision-language models with 3D scene understanding, avoiding orientation search while maintaining holistic spatial context.

Sound technical pipeline: The combination of structure-aware camera placement (balancing coverage, surface clearance, and trajectory proximity), zero-conv adapter feature injection (geometric and semantic features), EMD coordinate loss, and visibility-aware 3D aggregation via geometric consensus is well-designed and coherent.

Comprehensive empirical validation: Demonstrates state-of-the-art results on both Nr3D and ScanRefer, outperforming specialized 3D grounding frameworks as well as large zero-shot proprietary VLM setups.

Thorough generalization and ablation studies: Evaluates cross-dataset transfer (ARKitScenes, 3RScan) and robustness against textual variations (paraphrasing, affordances, and target noun masking). Extensive ablations, including an insightful direct comparison between panoramic and pinhole views, layer probing, and real-world deployment from iPhone captures with 3DGS, solidly substantiate each architectural choice.
weaknesses: High computational latency during inference: Performing multiple forward passes per query (averaging ~9.6 forward passes across viewpoints and yaw rotations) with large VLM backbones like CogVLM-17B leads to notable latency (~3.3 seconds per query on an A100 GPU), which may constrain interactive real-time robotics applications.

Dependency on multi-stage modular components: The framework relies on a multi-step pipeline requiring prior 3D reconstruction, feature lifting, off-the-shelf 2D instance segmentation (SAM), and geometric lifting/filtering, making deployment more complex than direct end-to-end 3D or 2D models.
Evaluation metric scope on ScanRefer: Tab. 1 reports Acc@0.25 on ScanRefer; providing Acc@0.5 alongside Acc@0.25 would give a more complete picture of high-precision 3D box localization performance.

strengths: Compelling intermediate representation: Using equirectangular panoramic renderings effectively bridges 2D vision-language models and 3D scene understanding. A 360-degree field of view avoids the viewpoint-truncation pitfalls of pinhole cameras and allows the VLM to observe long-range inter-object relationships simultaneously.

Well-designed technical components: The paper introduces well-motivated design choices across the entire pipeline, including structure-aware camera placement that balances ray coverage and surface clearance, multi-modal feature injection (depth geometry and multi-view lifted semantics) via zero-initialized adapters, and an Earth Mover's Distance (EMD) loss tailored for numeric coordinate token regression.

Strong empirical performance: PanoGrounder achieves state-of-the-art results on Nr3D (74.6%, outperforming ViewSRD by +4.7%) and ScanRefer (61.0% single-dataset, 62.0% joint-dataset), as well as convincing zero-shot performance (53.2% on Nr3D) that outperforms larger proprietary/open backbones like GPT-4V and Qwen2-VL-72B.

Extensive generalization and robustness experiments: The evaluation is thorough, including cross-dataset transfer to ARKitScenes and 3RScan, robustness under challenging textual modifications (paraphrases, affordance-only, noun-masked queries), and direct comparisons between panoramic and pinhole camera setups (Table 6).

Detailed implementation and practical analysis in the supplementary: The paper includes extensive analysis of backbone scalability (Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B vs. CogVLM-17B), test-time augmentation, adapter layer placements, and an end-to-end real-world deployment on an iPhone video using COLMAP and 3DGS.
weaknesses: Computational cost and inference latency: Feeding multi-view panoramic renderings (averaging 2.4 camera locations with 4 yaw rotations = 9.6 passes per query) into a 17B VLM leads to relatively high online per-query latency (3.30 s) and GPU memory footprint (51.6 GB) compared to native, feed-forward 3D point cloud backbones.

Dependency on multi-stage 3D reconstruction preprocessing: The pipeline requires pre-existing textured 3D meshes or pre-trained 3D Gaussian Splatting representations along with depth extraction and feature projection. In uncurated real-world scans, reconstruction artifacts or floater Gaussians can degrade the rendered panoramas and hurt downstream 2D grounding.

Disconnect between benchmark evaluation protocols: The paper employs 2D-to-3D mask unprojection via SAM for free-form box regression (ScanRefer), but switches to a two-stage candidate proposal matching and voting heuristic for ReferIt3D (Nr3D/Sr3D). A unified formulation would be cleaner and more consistent.

Vulnerability to equirectangular distortions and extreme aspect ratios: Bounding boxes defined in equirectangular coordinates can suffer from severe spherical distortions, especially near the poles (high/low elevation angles), requiring reliance on fine-tuning and post-processing SAM unprojection.
